title: Effect of high-fat, high-protein, and high-carbohydrate meals on the pharmacokinetics of a small dose of ethanol

claims.statement: In 9 healthy non-smoking men (mean age 24.6) in a Swedish laboratory, each given the same small amount of alcohol (0.30 g per kg of body weight, diluted to 20% in orange juice and drunk within 15 minutes; study conditions) on five occasions at least a week apart in random order (Jones et al., 1997), drinking a few minutes after a breakfast of about 3,000 kJ, compared with drinking after a 10-hour overnight fast, reduced the peak blood alcohol concentration and the area under the blood-alcohol curve over 210 minutes by roughly half: peaks were 16.6, 17.7 and 13.3 mg/dl after breakfasts rich in fat, carbohydrate and protein, against 30.8 mg/dl after fasting (43 to 57 in 100 of the fasting peak; editors' calculation), and the areas 1,767, 1,619 and 1,270 against 3,210 mg/dl·min (40 to 55 in 100); the same dose infused into a vein gave a peak of 54.3 mg/dl. No test of each breakfast against fasting is printed, but by the editors' estimate each difference is several times its standard error. The three breakfasts did not differ significantly, but that comparison had little power (0.22 and 0.25, and the authors call for caution), and the protein-rich breakfast, which also had about 9 in 100 more energy, gave peaks 20 to 25 in 100 lower than the other two (editors' calculation), so the study cannot show whether the kind of food matters. After the fat- and carbohydrate-rich breakfasts the peak came 30 to 90 minutes after drinking (30 to 60 after the protein-rich one and after fasting), and after food it varied more between men (coefficients of variation 24 to 40 in 100, against 14 after fasting). The authors explain the lower values by slower emptying of the stomach letting the liver break down more alcohol before it reaches the blood, or by part of the alcohol being held by the meal; neither was measured, and their statement that alcohol left the blood 1 to 2 hours sooner after food comes from looking at the curves, not from a measurement. The study gave one small amount, to young men only, measured no impairment, and did not test larger amounts, women, other meals or longer gaps between eating and drinking. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Jones et al. (1997), n = 9, mean (SD): peak mg/dl, fat-rich 16.6 (4.0), carbohydrate-rich 17.7 (7.1), protein-rich 13.3 (4.0), fasting 30.8 (4.3), intravenous 54.3 (6.4); AUC 0–210 min, mg/dl·min, 1,767 (549), 1,619 (760), 1,270 (406), 3,210 (527), 4,786 (446). Five conditions: F = 98.7 (peak) and 88.9 (AUC), P < 0.001; three meals: F = 2.22 and 2.42, P > 0.05, post hoc power 0.22 and 0.25. Time to peak 30–90 min (fat- and carbohydrate-rich), 30–60 min (protein-rich, fasting), 30 min (intravenous). Coefficients of variation: peak 24–40% after meals, 14% fasting; AUC 31–47% and 16%. Editors' calculations: meal peaks 43–57% and AUCs 40–55% of the fasting values; protein-rich peak about 20% and 25% lower than fat- and carbohydrate-rich, AUC about 28% and 22% lower; each meal–fasting difference about 5 to 9 times its approximate standard error (five-condition residual SD, assuming sphericity).
